headline: Frost is near — keep row cover or old sheets ready to protect tender crops this week.

tasks.title: Frost watch
tasks.detail: First frost on the Seacoast typically lands around mid-October. Check the nightly low each evening and drape row cover or old bedsheets over tomatoes, peppers, and basil whenever it dips toward the mid-30s.

tasks.title: Bring in warm-season crops
tasks.detail: Pick all peppers and the last tomatoes now — even full-size green tomatoes will ripen on a counter indoors. Harvest winter squash once the rind is hard and cure it in a warm, dry spot for a week.

tasks.title: Plant garlic
tasks.detail: Early-to-mid October is prime garlic planting in zone 6a. Break a bulb into cloves and set them pointy-end up, 2 inches deep and 6 inches apart, then top with a few inches of straw mulch.

tasks.title: Keep cutting cool-season greens
tasks.detail: Kale, spinach, lettuce, chard, and arugula keep producing and actually sweeten after a light frost. Harvest outer leaves regularly to keep plants going into November.

tasks.title: Sow a cover crop or plant bulbs
tasks.detail: On any bed you're done with, scatter winter rye to protect the soil over winter. It's also the window to tuck in spring bulbs like daffodils and tulips before the ground freezes.

tasks.title: Clear spent, diseased foliage
tasks.detail: Pull and discard (don't compost) any blighted tomato vines or mildewed squash leaves. Removing diseased debris now reduces the pests and spores that overwinter and hit you next spring.
